extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of journalism and media history
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and historical evaluation of tabloid newspapers and related newspaper-industry developments (circulation, advertising, labor, radio) in the U.S. from 1914–1940. Focuses on characteristics, business tactics, ethical issues, and technological adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern tabloid characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloid journalism in 1940 had come to stand for, in general, three things: (1) the folded-in-half page-size, in comparison with that of the normal eight-column paper; (2) the devotion of a large proportion of the paper’s space, including its front page, to pictures; and (3) a terse, condensed, and lively presentation of the news, usually disregarding the old 'summary lead' style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three traits are presented as the defining criteria of the modern tabloid form: compact physical format, pictorial emphasis (front-page illustrations, halftone pictures), and a short, snappy style that favors condensation over traditional summary leads. Use these measures to identify and evaluate tabloids historically or comparatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page pictorial emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The first page was given over to illustration; halftone news pictures and popular features dominated the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A front page dominated by photographs/illustrations—especially halftones—indicates tabloid positioning and strategy. Practically, such pictorial emphasis increases readability in crowded public spaces (e.g., subway trains) and shapes story selection toward visually striking material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terse, condensed, and lively presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A terse, condensed, and lively presentation of the news, usually disregarding the old 'summary lead' style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, snappy writing that condenses information and abandons the classical summary-lead structure is a stylistic criterion for tabloids. It promotes quick consumption (useful on public transit) but can de-emphasize depth and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensational/crime-and-sex content as circulation driver
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper abandoned the more conservative Tribune tradition and, trying crime-and-sex sensation, had found it well adapted to both pictorial treatment and the short, snappy style of tabloid journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of sensational crime and sexual scandal is identified as an explicit editorial tactic to drive circulation. While effective for rapid growth, it raises ethical risks (invasion of privacy, obscenity) and can provoke organized backlash ('holy war' led by educational and church agencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional tactics (contests, coupon prizes, Sunday editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contests and coupon prizes, and the addition of a Sunday edition, stimulated circulation growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotions such as contests and coupon incentives, plus product extensions like Sunday editions, are practical business criteria for increasing readership. They are cited as concrete tactics behind rapid circulation gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business/organizational practices supporting success
rubrics_metrics.description: Generous bonuses to employees have been the rule on the Daily News, and some fifty editorial workers own Tribune Company stock. Annual profits run into the millions. The paper moved into a new $10,000,000 home— one of the world's finest newspaper buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employee incentives, internal stock ownership, profitable operations, and investment in facilities/press capacity are management-level criteria indicating a paper's commercial health and stability. These practices also contribute to staff loyalty and product quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of newspaper health: circulation, advertising, profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate daily circulation and total newspaper advertising are used as key industry indicators; circulation figures (e.g., hundreds of thousands to millions) and advertising totals (hundreds of millions of dollars) measure success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative metrics—circulation size, advertising revenue, and profits—are primary evaluative standards for newspapers. Historical examples (circulation milestones, advertising share shifts) illustrate how to compare papers and industry health across periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational stabilization: 'stoop to conquer' editorial shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Like other great newspapers in former years, the News tended to abandon extreme sensationalism after it had gained a large following by the 'stoop to conquer' technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An observed pattern: papers that initially used sensationalism to grow often moderated content once established, shifting toward issues of broader public concern. This editorial moderation is a criterion for long-term reputational consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/anti-patterns of tabloid excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Excesses included reckless sensationalism, ruthless invasions of privacy, picture faking (composograph), and publication of obscene or indecent material, provoking legal actions and social campaigns against 'Daily Pornographic' journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit anti-patterns: practices that can produce legal liability (libel, obscenity), loss of public trust, court suits, and organized social pressure. Recording such instances is important when evaluating a paper's ethics and sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' news selection bias toward scandalous material
rubrics_metrics.description: In this newspaper situation, the competitive tabloids watched keenly for the appearance of their malodorous materials; the competitive tabloids watched keenly for the appearance of their malodorous materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for editorial behavior: active pursuit and aggregation of sensational, scandalous, or visually arresting stories. While effective for front-page impact, this selection bias should be weighed against accuracy, verification, and legal/ethical exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: N.R.A. newspaper code considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The daily newspaper code formation under the National Industrial Recovery Act raised objections because it seemed to be, in effect, a licensing of newspapers by government and therefore a threat to liberty of the press; the A.N.P.A. committee insisted upon inserting in the newspaper code a statement of the constitutional guarantee of the freedom of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming industry codes or voluntary agreements, include explicit protections for press freedom to counter perceptions of government licensing. The short life of the daily code (15 months) and the Supreme Court invalidation of the underlying Act are historical cautions about legal and constitutional vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor/union objectives and measures of success (American Newspaper Guild)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Newspaper Guild was organized 'to preserve the vocational interests of its members and to improve the conditions under which they work by collective bargaining, and to raise the standards of journalism.' Guild success is measured by recognition, salary-scale readjustments, and sometimes closed shops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate labor organizations by their stated aims (vocational protection, working-condition improvements, raising standards) and by outcomes (contracts negotiated, recognition obtained, strikes, affiliation with larger labor bodies). Publisher opposition and union strategies (boycotts, strikes) are relevant context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press unions and mechanical staff protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of the typographical and pressmen’s unions prevented reduction in average wages on the mechanical side during the depression and even won advances, accomplished with comparatively few strikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical-side unions' bargaining power is a structural criterion affecting newspaper operating costs, production continuity, and labor stability. Historical labor relations are important when assessing industry resilience in downturns.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP/newsgathering and radio-broadcasting policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Associated Press warned members against broadcasting their news (1922); rules were relaxed in 1925 to allow use of news 'of transcendent national or international importance'; in 1928 AP/UP/INS united to give radio two daily broadcasts and enlarged concessions in 1929; AP joined other agencies in allowing use of its reports on sponsored newscasts only in 1939.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News agencies' syndication and broadcast policies set explicit criteria for what material may be repurposed for radio—initially highly restrictive, later progressively permissive. Use this as a rubric to judge when and how wire news was authorized for radio, and the competitive/preventive rationales behind agency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper ownership of radio stations and effect on circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: By 1940 nearly 250 stations were owned by or affiliated with newspapers (about a third of the total), and the conviction grew that newscasting did little harm to newspaper circulation—sometimes it actually stimulated street sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership of radio stations by newspapers is an adaptive strategy; evaluate its impact by station counts, cross-promotion effects, and evidence of circulation stimulation versus advertising revenue cannibalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of new technologies (television, facsimile) for newspaper business
rubrics_metrics.description: Television broadcasts (cathode-ray) beginning in 1939 were limited to a radius of about thirty miles and seemed to adapt these broadcasts to local rather than national advertising; experiments in facsimile newspaper pages by radio were carried out (St. Louis Post-Dispatch, McClatchy, Dallas Morning News).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological suitability criteria: geographic reach (e.g., TV local radius), advertising market fit (local vs national), and experimental viability (facsimile transmission trials). These determine whether and how newspapers should invest in emergent broadcast/telemetry technologies.
